prohibited_recommendations: Do not conclude bitemporal epilepsy from the outpatient bilateral temporal findings or the right temporal slowing: all 17 recorded seizures arose from the left temporal region.
Do not continue indefinite ASM escalation without surgical evaluation once drug-resistance criteria are met.
Do not plan a resection limited to the hippocampus: the associated temporopolar abnormality should be included to reduce the risk of seizure recurrence.
Do not read the low-normal lamotrigine level as non-adherence: carbamazepine induction lowers lamotrigine.
required_recommendations: Present him at the multidisciplinary epilepsy surgery conference for left anterior temporal resection: two appropriately chosen and tolerated ASM schedules have failed (ILAE 2010), and MRI, video-EEG and neuropsychology concordantly point to the left temporal lobe.

Plan a resection that includes the left temporal pole with the hippocampus and amygdala (anterior temporal lobectomy rather than selective amygdalohippocampectomy), after language lateralization, with counseling on the risk of verbal memory and naming decline in the language-dominant hemisphere.
While awaiting surgery, add a non-inducing ASM (for example lacosamide or clobazam) rather than another enzyme inducer, and monitor sodium on carbamazepine.
Counsel on SUDEP risk and how seizure control reduces it.
Advise no driving until the locally applicable seizure-free interval is met and explain the duty to inform the licensing authority; review classroom safety before he returns to teaching.

avoided_actions.rationale: A six-year stereotyped focal epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis, no fever, no subacute cognitive decline and no immunosuppression: no indication for lumbar puncture.

All 17 recorded habitual events had a left temporal electrographic seizure correlate.
Six-year stereotyped course with unilateral hippocampal atrophy rather than swelling, and no subacute cognitive or psychiatric change.
The temporopolar abnormality has no mass effect, cyst or nodular component on 3T MRI.

key_clinical_evidence: Six years of stereotyped seizures (epigastric rising, deja vu, lip smacking, right-hand fumbling, two bilateral tonic-clonic seizures) with failure of levetiracetam at 1500 mg twice daily for a year and of lamotrigine with carbamazepine at therapeutic levels: drug-resistant epilepsy (ILAE 2010); the oxcarbazepine trial, stopped for hyponatremia, was uninformative.
3T epilepsy-protocol MRI: left hippocampal sclerosis with left temporopolar gray-white blurring, possibly FCD type IIIa, which the outside 1.5T standard MRI had not shown.

Video-EEG recorded 17 habitual seizures, all of left anterior temporal onset, with left anterior temporal sharp waves; the right temporal slowing and the bilateral outpatient findings do not indicate a right-sided focus.
Verbal memory and naming deficits with preserved visual memory fit left temporal dysfunction and frame the surgical risk.
A lamotrigine level of 3.2 mcg/mL on 200 mg twice daily reflects carbamazepine induction, not non-adherence.
Concordant MRI, video-EEG and neuropsychology make him a candidate for left anterior temporal resection that includes the temporal pole.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Johnson is a 47-year-old right-handed African American man with a six-year history of focal epilepsy presenting for inpatient video-EEG monitoring as part of a surgical evaluation. His seizures began at age 41 with a stereotyped sequence: an intense rising sensation in his epigastrium and an overpowering sense of deja vu lasting 5 to 10 seconds, followed by loss of awareness and repetitive automatisms consisting of lip smacking and fumbling movements of his right hand. Postictal confusion typically lasts 10 to 20 minutes. His wife reports that during episodes he sometimes turns his head slowly to the right and makes chewing movements, and he has on two occasions secondarily generalized to bilateral tonic-clonic activity with tongue biting.

At the time of initial diagnosis six years ago, he was evaluated at an outside hospital where a standard-protocol MRI of the brain was reported as normal and a routine 30-minute EEG was described as 'mild diffuse slowing, no epileptiform discharges.' He was diagnosed with focal epilepsy of unknown etiology and started on levetiracetam, titrated to 1500 mg twice daily; over the following year he continued to have one to two seizures a month despite good adherence, and it was then stopped because of irritability and low mood. Oxcarbazepine was started next but caused symptomatic hyponatremia within two months, requiring discontinuation. His current regimen of lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily plus carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily was started 18 months ago and initially reduced seizure frequency from approximately weekly to two to three per month. Over the past three months, however, seizures have increased to approximately four to six per week despite confirmed adherence. He denies any recent changes in sleep, alcohol intake, illness, or new medications. His wife notes that some episodes resolve within 30 seconds while others last up to two minutes.

He was referred to our comprehensive epilepsy center after a neurology outpatient visit. At that visit, a repeat outpatient EEG reportedly showed 'bilateral temporal slowing, greater on the left, with intermittent left and right temporal sharp transients of uncertain significance.' This ambiguous finding, combined with ongoing breakthrough seizures, prompted referral for inpatient evaluation. The patient and his family are motivated to pursue surgical evaluation given the functional impact of his epilepsy on his teaching career and independence. He has not driven for four years. He is admitted to the epilepsy monitoring unit for long-term video-EEG, updated MRI epilepsy protocol, and further evaluation.
